hypothesis: For a moderately complex, cross-functional business workflow (e.g., B2B customer onboarding), a coordinated multi-agent workflow orchestrated via an explicit orchestration layer (queue/state-machine based) will (a) improve task-level quality and throughput compared to a single generalist agent, while (b) keeping latency and cost within acceptable bounds for operations leaders (≤25% latency increase for at least 10% quality gain, or ≥20% throughput gain at similar quality).

baseline.description: Single-agent orchestration: a single generalist LLM-based agent is responsible for the entire workflow end-to-end, from intake to validation, drafting outputs, and quality checks. It uses tools directly (APIs to synthetic CRM/ERP/email), maintains its own ephemeral state per request, and there is no separate orchestration layer beyond a simple request/response call pattern.

architecture.agent_type: single generalist agent with tool-usage capabilities
architecture.orchestration: synchronous function call per workflow instance (e.g., HTTP POST or CLI call) with no intermediate queues or explicit state machine; the agent internally tracks progress via prompt state only
architecture.state_management: per-request in-memory context; no shared state store other than logs
tools: synthetic_Risk_API (returns risk scores and KYC flags)
synthetic_Email_API (simulated outbound email draft generation only; no actual sends)
architecture.communication_pattern: agent interacts only with tools; no other agents involved
architecture.error_handling: basic retries at the tool-call layer; no explicit workflow compensation logic

treatment.description: Multi-agent workflow with an explicit orchestration layer: the workflow is decomposed into distinct agent roles (router, specialist, reviewer, supervisor) coordinated through a simple orchestration layer implemented as a combination of a task queue and a state-machine controller. Each agent operates on shared workflow state persisted in a store, and communication occurs via structured messages.

agents.name: RouterAgent
agents.role: Initial intake, classification of onboarding requests, and routing decisions (e.g., standard vs. high-risk customers; required checks).
capabilities: natural language understanding of intake forms/emails
mapping to standardized workflow types and SLAs
adding routing metadata to shared state

agents.name: DataEnrichmentAgent
agents.role: Collects and verifies customer data from CRM and risk tools; enriches missing fields.
capabilities: normalizes enrichment results into structured JSON
flags inconsistencies or missing required data

agents.name: ContractDraftingAgent
agents.role: Generates a draft service agreement or order form based on customer profile and risk classification.
capabilities: returns a draft contract summary and structured terms

agents.name: QualityReviewerAgent
agents.role: Performs an automated quality and compliance review across enriched data and draft contract; suggests corrections.
capabilities: identifies potential inconsistencies or risk rule violations
emits a structured review report with pass/fail and reasons

agents.name: SupervisorAgent
agents.role: Final decision logic: accepts or rejects the workflow outcome, requests rework from specific agents, or escalates for human review.
capabilities: reads shared workflow state and previous agent outputs
decides next state in state machine (e.g., DONE, REWORK_ENRICHMENT)
triggers delegation by posting tasks back to orchestration layer

orchestration.pattern: central orchestrator with per-workflow state machine and message queue
components: WorkflowStateStore (e.g., SQLite/Postgres or in-memory DB for tests)
TaskQueue (simple FIFO in code, or Redis/RabbitMQ/Kafka for production-like setups)
OrchestratorService (state-machine controller routing tasks to agents)

transitions: any_state -> ESCALATED (SupervisorAgent deems human review necessary)

state_management.store_type: SQLite (default for reproducibility) with an ORM or lightweight DAL

architecture.communication_pattern: agents communicate indirectly via shared state and task queue; each task includes a workflow_id, target_agent, and an operation type (e.g., ENRICH, REVIEW). No direct agent-to-agent calls.

error_handling.dead_letter_queue: failed_tasks table or topic for post-hoc analysis
error_handling.loop_protection: max_state_transitions_per_workflow=20; loop detection via repeated cycles between the same states
error_handling.conflict_resolution: last-writer-wins with conflict logs; experiments log all conflicts for analysis

workloads.name: synthetic_customer_onboarding_standard
workloads.description: Synthetic B2B customer onboarding cases representing standard risk, complete data, and straightforward pricing. Simulates a SaaS vendor onboarding mid-market B2B customers.

ground_truth.description: Reference outputs derived from a combination of human-designed rules and LLM-generated solutions validated by the author. Includes target enriched profile, risk classification, and target contract summary.

workloads.name: synthetic_customer_onboarding_high_risk
workloads.description: Synthetic onboarding cases with incomplete data, higher regulatory or credit risk flags, and edge-case pricing/terms that stress test routing and review behavior.

ground_truth.description: Reference outputs specifying correct escalations, additional checks, and conservative contract terms for risky customers.

workloads.name: synthetic_customer_onboarding_mixed_batch
workloads.description: Mixed stream of standard and high-risk onboarding cases simulating a real queue over a fixed time window. Used for throughput experiments.

ground_truth.description: Merged ground truth labels for both standard and high-risk cases tagged by segment.

llm_and_tools.llm_provider: Same LLM family and version across baseline and treatment (e.g., OpenAI gpt-4o-mini or equivalent). If using open-source models, same checkpoint and inference parameters.
llm_and_tools.tool_implementations: Identical Python functions and back-end behavior for synthetic_CRM_API, synthetic_Risk_API, synthetic_Contracts_API, synthetic_Email_API, synthetic_Knowledge_API across both conditions.

prompting.business_rules: Identical business rules and policy descriptions provided to all agents; single-agent baseline receives combined guidance, while multi-agent system receives role-specific excerpts sourced from the same canonical policy files.
prompting.evaluation_prompts: Automatic evaluators (where used, e.g., LLM-as-judge) must use the same prompts and models for scoring baseline and treatment outputs.

compute_and_environment.hardware: Run all experiments on the same class of machine (e.g., 4 vCPU, 16GB RAM) or same Kubernetes node pool type.
compute_and_environment.concurrency: Limit concurrent workflow executions to the same fixed level (e.g., 10 parallel workflows) for both baseline and treatment in throughput experiments.
compute_and_environment.rate_limits: Apply identical LLM and tool rate limits (QPS caps) in both conditions.

case_assignment.randomization: For each workload, randomly shuffle the list of case_ids and then assign identical sequences to baseline and treatment runs.
case_assignment.runs_per_condition: At least 3 full runs per workload and condition to average out stochastic LLM variance; re-seed randomness per run deterministically.

governance.no_human_intervention: During benchmark runs, no manual corrections or overrides are allowed. Human inspection is used only for post-hoc evaluation and labeling (if needed), not during execution.
governance.frozen_code: Tag a release in the repository (e.g., `ch06-experiments-v1`) and ensure both baseline and treatment experiments use that tag.

metrics.name: workflow_success_rate
metrics.description: Fraction of workflows that reach a DONE state without escalation or failure and meet minimum quality thresholds.

metrics.name: escalation_rate
metrics.description: Fraction of workflows that the system flags for human review or escalation.

metrics.name: average_end_to_end_latency
metrics.description: Average wall-clock time from workflow intake to DONE/ESCALATED/FAILED.

metrics.name: median_end_to_end_latency
metrics.description: Median wall-clock time from workflow intake to DONE/ESCALATED/FAILED.

metrics.name: throughput
metrics.description: Number of workflows completed (DONE or ESCALATED) per unit time under a fixed concurrency configuration.

metrics.name: quality_score_enrichment
metrics.description: Accuracy of enriched customer profiles compared to ground truth.

metrics.name: quality_score_risk_classification
metrics.description: Accuracy of risk category and escalation decisions compared to ground truth.

metrics.name: quality_score_contract_summary
metrics.description: Semantic quality and correctness of contract summaries vs. ground truth, as measured by a rubric or LLM-as-judge.

metrics.name: tool_call_count
metrics.description: Average total number of tool calls per workflow (summed across all tools).

metrics.name: llm_token_usage
metrics.description: Total LLM token usage per workflow across all prompts and responses.

metrics.name: estimated_llm_cost
metrics.description: Estimated monetary cost of LLM usage based on a configurable price per 1K tokens.

metrics.name: state_transitions_per_workflow
metrics.description: Number of state transitions a workflow instance goes through (proxy for orchestration overhead and complexity).

metrics.name: rework_rate
metrics.description: Fraction of workflows that required at least one rework cycle (e.g., REWORK_NEEDED state).

metrics.name: deadlock_or_loop_rate
metrics.description: Fraction of workflows that were terminated due to loop detection or exceeding max transitions.

metrics.name: conflicting_actions_rate
metrics.description: Fraction of workflows where conflicting actions (e.g., contradictory writes) between agents were detected.

primary: On the mixed_batch workload, the multi-agent treatment achieves at least a 10 percentage point improvement in either quality_score_risk_classification or quality_score_contract_summary over the single-agent baseline, OR at least a 20% increase in throughput, while keeping average_end_to_end_latency increase ≤25% relative to baseline.
workflow_success_rate for the multi-agent treatment is not more than 5 percentage points lower than baseline; ideally it is higher.
secondary: escalation_rate is lower or equal in the multi-agent treatment for standard cases; for high-risk cases, a higher but more accurate escalation_rate is acceptable if matched by improved risk classification accuracy.
rework_rate in the multi-agent system remains ≤30% unless accompanied by clear improvements in final quality metrics.
deadlock_or_loop_rate and conflicting_actions_rate are both <1% of workflows in the multi-agent system.
success_criteria.business_interpretation: For operations leaders, the multi-agent pattern is considered beneficial if it either (a) raises quality at acceptable latency and cost, making it suitable for high-stakes workflows, or (b) significantly improves throughput at comparable quality, making it suitable for high-volume, moderate-risk workflows.

technical: Deadlocks or livelocks in the multi-agent state machine (e.g., infinite cycling between REWORK_NEEDED and ENRICHED).
Excessive orchestration overhead causing higher latency and cost without quality or throughput gains.
Race conditions or conflicting actions when multiple agents write to shared state concurrently.
Message or task loss in the queue implementation leading to stuck workflows.
Agent prompt misalignment causing agents to duplicate work or ignore state (e.g., ContractDraftingAgent ignoring enriched risk flags).
behavioral: Over-fragmentation of roles leading to brittle workflows that break when scenarios deviate slightly from training cases.
Excessive escalations in the multi-agent system that negate automation value.
Specialist agents becoming too narrow and failing to handle cross-cutting logic that the single-agent baseline handled correctly.
measurement_and_experimental: Non-comparable workloads due to misaligned random seeds or different test subsets between conditions.
Evaluator bias if LLM-as-judge favors more verbose or structured outputs (common in multi-agent treatment) over minimal but correct single-agent outputs.
Incorrect or inconsistent ground truth labels, particularly for contract summaries and escalation decisions.
mitigations: Implement strict max_state_transitions_per_workflow and log any workflows terminated for loop protection.
Add conflict detection in the WorkflowStateStore (e.g., optimistic concurrency control) and log all conflicts.
Validate datasets and ground truth with scripted sanity checks (e.g., all case_ids aligned across inputs and labels).
Use blinded evaluation prompts where LLM-as-judge is not informed whether an output came from baseline or treatment.
Run pilot dry-runs on a subset (e.g., 20 cases) before full experiments to catch orchestration logic bugs.

software: Poetry or pip-based virtualenv for dependency management
Key dependencies (specified in pyproject.toml or requirements.txt):
- FastAPI or Flask (if running orchestrator as a service; optional for local batch mode)
- Redis or local queue library (if using Redis-backed task queues; otherwise an in-process queue implementation is provided)
- HTTP client library (e.g., httpx or requests) for LLM and tool calls
- pydantic or dataclasses-json for schema validation
- numpy/pandas for metric aggregation and analysis
infrastructure: Local developer machine or cloud VM with at least 4 vCPUs and 16 GB RAM.
Access to chosen LLM endpoint (cloud or local model server) configured via environment variables (e.g., OPENAI_API_KEY).
SQLite database file (default) or Postgres if desired, pre-configured in configs/ch06_*.yaml.
Optional: Redis instance if using Redis-backed TaskQueue implementation.

paths: schemas/ch06/ (JSON schemas for inputs, workflow state, and outputs)
notebooks/ch06/ (optional analysis notebooks for plotting results)

configuration.seeding: Use a deterministic random seed (e.g., 42) for workload shuffling and any stochastic control flows where applicable; seed is configurable via CLI flag or config file.

run_instructions:
1. Clone the repository and check out the experiment tag:
   - git clone https://github.com/bookauthority/turn-your-company-into-an-agentic-organization.git
   - cd turn-your-company-into-an-agentic-organization
   - git checkout ch06-experiments-v1   # or the tag specified in the book

2. Set up Python environment and install dependencies:
   - python -m venv .venv
   - source .venv/bin/activate  # Windows: .venv\\Scripts\\activate
   - pip install -r requirements.txt  # or `poetry install` if using Poetry

3. Configure environment variables:
   - export LLM_PROVIDER=openai
   - export LLM_MODEL_NAME=gpt-4o-mini  # or another supported model
   - export OPENAI_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY_HERE
   - export DB_URL=sqlite:///./ch06_experiments.db
   - export QUEUE_BACKEND=in_memory  # or redis if configured
   - export RANDOM_SEED=42

4. Validate datasets and schemas:
   - python experiments/ch06/validate_datasets.py \
       --input-dir data/ch06/onboarding \
       --schema-dir schemas/ch06
   This should report zero schema validation errors before proceeding.

5. Run the single-agent baseline for each workload:
   - python experiments/ch06/run_single_agent.py \
       --config configs/ch06_single_agent.yaml \
       --workload standard_cases \
       --runs 3 \
       --output-dir results/ch06/baseline/standard
   - python experiments/ch06/run_single_agent.py \
       --config configs/ch06_single_agent.yaml \
       --workload high_risk_cases \
       --runs 3 \
       --output-dir results/ch06/baseline/high_risk
   - python experiments/ch06/run_single_agent.py \
       --config configs/ch06_single_agent.yaml \
       --workload mixed_cases \
       --runs 3 \
       --output-dir results/ch06/baseline/mixed

6. Run the multi-agent treatment for each workload:
   - python experiments/ch06/run_multi_agent.py \
       --config configs/ch06_multi_agent.yaml \
       --workload standard_cases \
       --runs 3 \
       --output-dir results/ch06/multi_agent/standard
   - python experiments/ch06/run_multi_agent.py \
       --config configs/ch06_multi_agent.yaml \
       --workload high_risk_cases \
       --runs 3 \
       --output-dir results/ch06/multi_agent/high_risk
   - python experiments/ch06/run_multi_agent.py \
       --config configs/ch06_multi_agent.yaml \
       --workload mixed_cases \
       --runs 3 \
       --output-dir results/ch06/multi_agent/mixed

7. Compute metrics and compare baseline vs. treatment:
   - python experiments/ch06/aggregate_metrics.py \
       --baseline-dir results/ch06/baseline \
       --treatment-dir results/ch06/multi_agent \
       --ground-truth-dir data/ch06/onboarding \
       --output-file results/ch06/summary_metrics.json
   This script calculates metrics defined in this spec for each workload and condition.

8. (Optional) Run qualitative or LLM-as-judge evaluations of contract summaries:
   - python experiments/ch06/evaluate_contract_quality.py \
       --results-dir results/ch06 \
       --ground-truth-dir data/ch06/onboarding \
       --model-name $LLM_MODEL_NAME \
       --output-file results/ch06/contract_quality_scores.json

9. Analyze and visualize the results (optional but recommended):
   - jupyter notebook notebooks/ch06/analyze_ch06_experiments.ipynb
   Use the notebook to load results/ch06/summary_metrics.json and visualize differences in quality, latency, throughput, and cost.

10. Document observations:
   - Record which configuration variants (e.g., fewer/more agents, different state-machine settings) you tried, along with their metric outcomes, in a markdown log (e.g., results/ch06/experiment_log.md) to support organizational decision-making.

summary_file.description: Top-level JSON file summarizing metrics by workload and condition.

per_run_files.description: Detailed logs and metrics per run, for debugging and deeper analysis.

audit_and_debug_logs.description: Optional detailed audit logs with per-step agent messages and state transitions used for diagnosing failure modes like deadlocks, loops, or conflicting actions.
